cases.title: Alabuga Start (Tatarstan drone factory recruitment)
cases.summary: Alabuga Start is a recruitment program promoted on social media that offers young foreign women, mostly aged 18–22 from countries including Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, South Sudan, Sierra Leone and Nigeria, plane tickets, money and work-study roles such as hospitality and catering. According to an AP investigation, many learned only after arriving at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan that they would assemble Iranian-designed attack drones, and described long surveilled shifts, broken wage promises, and chemical exposure. The US Treasury sanctioned SEZ Alabuga in February 2024, the EU requires EU operators to withdraw from the zone, and in May 2026 the UK designated people and entities involved in recruitment for Alabuga Start.

cases.title: Arup Hong Kong (deepfake CFO video call)
cases.summary: A staff member in engineering firm Arup's Hong Kong office received a message said to be from the company's UK-based chief financial officer about a confidential transaction, then joined a video conference with the false CFO and other AI-generated employees. The employee made transfers totalling about US$25 million to five Hong Kong bank accounts before discovering the fraud. Arup notified Hong Kong police in January 2024 and confirmed to the Financial Times that false voices and images were used. No one has been publicly charged.

cases.title: Bolaji Bolarinwa (domestic servitude, New Jersey)
cases.summary: Bolaji Bolarinwa of Moorestown, New Jersey recruited two women to come to the United States, one of them on a student visa, and then forced them to do household work and childcare in her home. According to DOJ, she lured them with false promises, confiscated their passports and used threats of physical harm (including to one victim's daughter), verbal and physical abuse, isolation and constant surveillance to make them work around the clock with minimal pay, from about December 2015 to October 2016. After a two-week trial she was found guilty of two counts of forced labor, one count of alien harboring for financial gain and two counts of document servitude. In May 2025 she was sentenced to 45 months in prison, three years of supervised release, a $35,000 fine and $87,518.72 in restitution.

cases.title: Brandon Sartor (multi-state sex trafficking)
cases.summary: Brandon Sartor of Prince George's County, Maryland initially recruited each victim by falsely promising to help them make money. From December 2024 to April 2025 he then compelled them to have sex with as many as 10 men a day across Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania and South Carolina, seizing the money. DOJ says he used punching and hitting, threats to harm or kill victims or their families, and opioids that he gave and withheld so victims feared withdrawal. In August 2026 Sartor pleaded guilty in the Southern District of Florida to two counts of sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion; sentencing was set for November 17, 2026, with a 15-year mandatory minimum.

cases.title: Brazil: Gisele Bündchen deepfake Instagram ads
cases.summary: Police in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, working with the financial intelligence unit COAF, arrested four suspects in October 2025 in an investigation that began in August 2024, after a victim reported an Instagram ad with an altered video of supermodel Gisele Bündchen promoting a skincare product. Another ad used her likeness to promise a giveaway of suitcases, with buyers paying shipping fees for items that never arrived. Investigators found more than 20 million reais (about US$3.9 million) in suspicious funds and froze assets across five states. Most victims lost under 100 reais and did not report it. These are arrests and allegations; no conviction was reported.

cases.title: Colombia's first domestic-servitude trafficking conviction (Vaupés to Bogotá)
cases.summary: In September 2018 a Colombian court handed down the country's first conviction for trafficking in persons for domestic servitude, sentencing a Colombian woman (not named by UNODC) to 13 years and 2 months. The victim, an 18-year-old Indigenous woman from Vaupés, was promised domestic work and a salary of US$77. On arrival in Bogotá she was told she would get no pay for two months to cover her travel tickets, then another 20 months unpaid for a decorative item she had broken. She worked over 12 hours a day with restrictions on her freedom. The prosecution argued abuse of a position of vulnerability, citing a UNODC issue paper.

cases.title: Delon Richard Smith (sex trafficking, Daytona Beach)
cases.summary: Delon Richard Smith of Daytona, Florida recruited two women separately in 2021 and 2022 by offering them narcotics and an opportunity to make money. He then used threats and severe physical violence, including punching, choking and assaults with a firearm, while referring to his membership in the Bloods gang, to compel them to engage in commercial sex in the Daytona Beach area. He posted online commercial sex advertisements featuring one victim's photograph and kept all the money. Smith pleaded guilty in October 2025 to two counts of sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion and one conspiracy count, and in February 2026 was sentenced to 327 months in prison and ordered to pay $4,800 in restitution.

cases.title: Dzaleka refugee camp trafficking network (Malawi)
cases.summary: UNODC and the Malawi Police Service report that a trafficking network used the Dzaleka Refugee Camp, 41 km from Lilongwe, as a hub. Agents in Ethiopia, the DRC and Burundi recruited people under false pretences, offering work in South Africa, and arranged their crossing into Malawi and entry into the camp; there they were told to pay off debts for being smuggled and were exploited in the camp or moved on for forced labour. Children were exploited for farm and domestic work and women and girls for sexual exploitation, in the camp, in Malawi and elsewhere in Southern Africa. After UNODC training, over 90 victims were identified and rescued, most of them Ethiopian men aged 18–30. As of May 2022 there were five arrests of suspects from Malawi, Ethiopia, Burundi, Rwanda and the DRC and cases were ongoing; police said victims' fear of testifying was hampering convictions. No one is named.

cases.title: Global Horizons Manpower (Thai farmworkers)
cases.summary: The EEOC alleged that between 2003 and 2007 Beverly Hills-based labor contractor Global Horizons brought Thai men to farms in Hawaii and Washington, charged them high recruitment fees that created insurmountable debt, confiscated passports, and housed them in dilapidated, crowded housing. In 2016 a federal judge in Washington awarded $7,658,500 against Global Horizons, and a companion Hawaii case produced a $12.3 million default judgment. A separate federal criminal case, United States v. Orian, was dismissed in July 2012 after the Justice Department said it could not prove the charged offenses beyond a reasonable doubt.

cases.title: Los Villatoros Harvesting (Mexican H-2A farmworkers)
cases.summary: Los Villatoros Harvesting (LVH), a farm labor contracting company, operated as a criminal enterprise between about 2015 and 2017. It fraudulently recruited Mexican nationals on short-term H-2A agricultural visas, charged exorbitant recruitment fees and lied about pay, hours, working conditions and expense reimbursement. In the US, workers were compelled to do long hours of farm labour six to seven days a week in Florida, Kentucky, Indiana, Georgia and North Carolina, for far less than they were owed. Coercion included imposed debts, confiscated passports, crowded and unsanitary housing, isolation, verbal abuse and threats of arrest, deportation and harm to family in Mexico. In June 2026 Alexander Villatoro Moreno was sentenced to 70 months in prison after pleading guilty to RICO conspiracy; company owner Bladimir Moreno had been sentenced to 118 months in 2022, and co-defendants received 41 months, 37 months and 8 months' home detention.

cases.title: Nepali migrants diverted to Malawi (Blantyre rescue)
cases.summary: According to UNODC, six Nepali nationals said they had been recruited through an agent about a year earlier and set out to reach the United States via Bolivia. Instead they were moved over months through Vietnam, Madagascar, Jordan, Dubai, Azerbaijan and Ethiopia (where they stayed four months), then brought to Malawi and told they would have to work there instead. They were locked in a house in Blantyre with their passports taken. Nepal's Anti-Human Trafficking Bureau, alerted by the families, tipped off Malawian police, who rescued the group on 6 November 2019. The victims were repatriated to Nepal and Malawian police said a Malawian suspect was arrested. UNODC describes them as presumed victims; no court outcome is reported and the agent is not named.

cases.title: AI voice-clone Biden robocalls (New Hampshire primary)
cases.summary: Two days before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary, voters received robocalls with an AI-generated voice imitating President Biden, spoofed to look as if they came from a prominent local Democrat. Political consultant Steve Kramer admitted creating the calls. Lingo Telecom, which carried them, agreed in August 2024 to a $1 million FCC fine and stronger caller-verification (STIR/SHAKEN) procedures, and in September 2024 the FCC fined Kramer $6 million. In June 2025 a New Hampshire jury found Kramer not guilty of state voter-suppression and candidate-impersonation charges. The case is included because it shows how convincing a cloned voice on a phone call can be.

cases.title: NXIVM (Keith Raniere) — sex trafficking and organized crime
cases.summary: NXIVM Corporation, founded by Keith Raniere, operated under the cover of a self-help and professional-development company. Federal investigations revealed an elaborate structure of coercive control, exploitation of female members, enforced debt bondage, and organized crime. Raniere and key associates were convicted in 2019–2021 on charges including racketeering, sex trafficking, forced labor, and financial crimes. The organization operated in the United States (NY, CA) and internationally (Mexico, Canada). Sayari and legal records show risk concentrated on individual leaders rather than the corporate shell, illustrating how small-business screening must traverse to beneficial owners.

cases.title: Operation Blooming Onion (USA v. Patricio et al.)
cases.summary: In November 2021 federal prosecutors in the Southern District of Georgia unsealed a 54-count indictment against 24 defendants, alleging a conspiracy that fraudulently used the H-2A visa program to bring workers from Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras to South Georgia farms. The indictment alleges workers were charged unlawful fees for transportation, food and housing, had travel and identity documents withheld, and were threatened with deportation and violence; at least two workers died. Prosecutors allege the conspirators made more than $200 million and laundered it through property, vehicles, businesses and a casino. These are allegations in an indictment; this record does not report individual case outcomes.

cases.title: Prince Group and Chen Zhi
cases.summary: Prince Holding Group, a Cambodia-based conglomerate chaired by Chen Zhi, is accused by US prosecutors of running forced-labor scam compounds across Cambodia where trafficked workers ran cryptocurrency investment ('pig butchering') frauds. On 14 October 2025 the US unsealed an indictment in Brooklyn charging Chen Zhi with wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy, filed a civil forfeiture complaint against about 127,271 bitcoin, and OFAC designated 146 targets as the Prince Group TCO in a joint action with the UK. Treasury said workers were lured by promises of well-paid customer service and tech support jobs. Chen Zhi remained at large at the time of the announcement.

cases.title: Signal International (Indian H-2B workers)
cases.summary: After Hurricane Katrina, Signal International used the H-2B program to bring nearly 500 men from India to work as welders and pipefitters in Mississippi and Texas; recruiters promised green cards and permanent residency, and workers paid $10,000–$20,000 or more in fees. Workers were charged $1,050 a month to live in overcrowded, guarded company camps. In February 2015 a New Orleans federal jury awarded $14 million to five workers, finding Signal and businesses of lawyer Malvern C. Burnett and recruiter Sachin Dewan liable for labor trafficking, fraud, racketeering and discrimination. In 2015 Signal agreed to a $20 million settlement resolving the SPLC-coordinated suits, including a $5 million EEOC settlement.

cases.title: Slovak crime group modern slavery case (UK)
cases.summary: A Slovak organised crime group recruited more than 60 Slovak nationals from the Košice and Prešov regions with promises of weekly salaries above EUR 400. In the UK, victims worked 14 hours a day, six days a week in restaurant kitchens and car washes for about EUR 25 a week and lived in poor conditions. After a UK–Slovak joint investigation team supported by Eurojust, five members were sentenced at Birmingham Crown Court to up to eight years for conspiracy to arrange human trafficking and compulsory labour.

cases.title: Worldwide Executive Job Search Solutions / PrivateEquityHeadhunters.com
cases.summary: The FTC alleged that Worldwide Executive Job Search Solutions, PrivateEquityHeadhunters.com and owner Craig Chrest messaged job seekers on LinkedIn and other networking sites, claiming access to unadvertised executive jobs at private equity and venture capital firms. Consumers paid upfront fees of $1,200 to $2,500, but the interviews and jobs were fictitious. A federal court in the Southern District of Texas froze assets in February 2019, and an October 2019 settlement permanently banned the defendants from offering employment services, with a $1,744,422 judgment of which all but $18,000 was suspended.
